item.title: Optimizing Database Queries in Spring Boot
Stop letting HikariCP kill your cheap database
item.description:
When you host a Spring Boot app on a ₹100/month tiny server, the default HikariCP settings will crash your database.
By default, Hikari sets the maximum pool size to 10. If you run three microservices, that is 30 active connections. PostgreSQL allocates a separate process for each connection, eating up precious RAM on your small VM.
You don't need 10 connections for low-to-medium traffic. Shrink your pool size and decrease the timeout so threads don't wait forever.
Update your `application.properties`:
```properties spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=3 spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=1 spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=5000 spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=120000 ```
This setup handles hundreds of API requests per second by quickly reusing connections. It keeps your database RAM usage low and prevents PostgreSQL from running out of memory.

item.title: Stop Using Identity Generation for Batch Inserts in Spring Boot
Stop Letting HikariCP Kill Your Cheap VPS
item.description:
Most developers launch Spring Boot on a cheap ₹100/month VPS and wonder why it crashes. The silent killer is often the default HikariCP connection pool.
By default, Hikari sets the maximum pool size to 10. Each active database connection consumes precious memory on both your app and database. If you run PostgreSQL, Redis and Spring Boot on a single 1GB RAM instance, this default setup quickly triggers the Linux OOM killer.
If your app doesn't handle massive concurrent writes, scale down. Limit the pool size to 2 or 3.
Update your `application.properties`:
```properties spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=3 spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=1 spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=10000 spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=30000 ```
This small tweak keeps your database footprint tiny, prevents crashes and lets you host full-stack apps on dirt-cheap hardware while scaling your initial revenue.

item.title: Run Spring Boot on a $1 VPS with GraalVM
item.description:
If you're hosting Spring Boot on cheap VPS plans, memory is your biggest bottleneck. A standard JVM app easily consumes 300MB to 500MB of RAM just sitting idle. That kills your budget if you want to run multiple services on a single cheap server.
The fix is compiling your application to a native binary using GraalVM. This drops startup time to milliseconds and cuts RAM usage to under 50MB.
You don't need complex configurations. Just add the GraalVM native buildtools plugin to your `pom.xml`:
```xml <plugin> <groupId>org.graalvm.buildtools</groupId> <artifactId>native-maven-plugin</artifactId> </plugin> ```
Then build your native image:
```bash mvn -Pnative native:compile ```
The compiler analyzes your code statically and removes unused classes, reflection overhead and heavy JVM startup processes. Your app now runs lightning fast on a tiny VPS, saving you hosting costs while handling traffic.

item.title: Stop over-allocating your HikariCP connection pool
item.description:
If you're hosting a Spring Boot app on a ₹100/month VPS, your default database pool configuration is probably killing your server.
By default, HikariCP grabs 10 connections. Each connection consumes database memory, socket buffers and thread overhead. On a tiny PostgreSQL instance, this drains resources fast.
To scale without crashing, reduce your pool size. For low-traffic apps running on cheap hardware, a pool of 3 connections is more than enough. You can handle hundreds of concurrent users if your queries are fast and non-blocking.
Update your `application.properties`:
```properties spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=3 spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=2 spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=30000 spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=5000 ```
This simple tweak slashes RAM usage, keeps your database healthy and lets you run your entire stack on a shoestring budget.

item.title: Catch Hidden Database Connection Leaks in Spring Boot
item.description:
If your API randomly hangs under load, you're likely leaking database connections. An unclosed resource or a slow network call inside a transaction can starve your HikariCP pool instantly.
Instead of hunting through code, make HikariCP point out the exact line holding connections too long.
Add this to your `application.yml`:
```yaml spring: datasource: hikari: leak-detection-threshold: 3000 ```
With this setting, if a thread retains a connection for more than 3000ms, HikariCP prints a stack trace showing where it happened.
We used this on a high-throughput payment worker hitting PostgreSQL, Redis and external gateways. It immediately flagged a third-party HTTP call executing inside an active transaction. Keep this threshold between 2000ms and 5000ms in production to catch bugs early.

item.title: Squeezing Spring Boot into a 1GB RAM VPS
item.description:
Host your Spring Boot app, PostgreSQL and Redis on a cheap $1.5/month VPS without getting killed by the Linux OOM reaper. By default, the JVM allocates memory aggressively, which leads to crashes on low-spec servers.
You can restrict the memory footprint using specific JVM flags in your startup script. This keeps the entire Spring Boot process under 350MB.
Run your jar like this:
```bash java -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 -Xms64m -Xmx256m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=128m -jar app.jar ```
Setting `ActiveProcessorCount=1` forces the JVM to size its internal thread pools for a single core. `Xms` and `Xmx` cap the heap memory.
Combine this with PostgreSQL memory tuning by lowering `shared_buffers` to 128MB and you can easily run your full stack on a micro VM. It keeps your hosting bill under ₹150 while you scale your MVP.
